reading.text:
Reading (locked before any Lean is shown) — def LevyStochCalc.Probability.aug

Paper notion (§2): "a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions ... The
filtration (F_t) is the usual augmentation of the one generated by W, N and an independent
initial σ-field F_0." The usual augmentation of a filtration (G_t) under P: F_t =
∩_{s > t} σ(G_s ∪ 𝒩), with 𝒩 the P-null sets (of the completed F, or of F_∞); this is
right-continuous and contains all null sets (equivalently σ(G_{t+} ∪ 𝒩)).

Faithful Lean definition: for each t, the σ-algebra ⨅_{s > t} (G_s ⊔ σ(null sets)), or
(⨅_{s>t} G_s) ⊔ σ(null sets), with null sets taken as the P-null measurable sets of the
ambient σ-algebra (since Lean's Ω carries one σ-algebra, adding null sets of the completion
not measurable in the ambient space is not possible; adding ambient-measurable null sets is
the standard Lean-level surrogate and is fine provided the ambient σ-algebra is what all
processes are measured against). Edge cases: at the end of the time index (if the index is
bounded, e.g. [0,T], ⨅ over the empty set gives ⊤ — must be capped at the ambient σ-algebra,
i.e. ≤ the ambient σ-algebra, otherwise it is not a filtration of the measurable space);
right-continuity must hold; null sets of P (not of some other measure). If aug only
completes (no right limit), the "usual conditions" claim fails (narrower: then results using
right-continuity, e.g. debut/stopping-time arguments, would be unavailable, but for the
statements it changes which processes are adapted).

comparison.text:
Comparison — aug (LevyStochCalc/Probability/Augmentation.lean:42-59)

Lean: aug m m₀ μ = {A : A ∈ m₀ ∧ ∃ B ∈ m, μ(A Δ B) = 0}, a σ-algebra (closure proofs given);
the file proves aug = m ⊔ σ(m₀-measurable μ-null sets) (aug_eq_sup_nullSigma) and that it
commutes with countable antitone infima.
Against my reading (usual augmentation: right-continuous and with all null sets):
- aug is only the null-set augmentation of one σ-algebra — no right limit. My reading flagged
  this as a problem IF aug were the paper's whole "usual augmentation". It is not used that
  way: the paper's filtration is enlJoint t = aug(((W,N)-natural ⊔ F_0)_{(max t 0)+}) m₀ P
  (Enlarged/Filtration.lean, Brownian.augFiltration of rightCont), i.e. right limit first, then
  null sets; this equals the textbook ⋂_{s>t} σ(G_s ∪ 𝒩) (limsup argument, which the file's
  aug_iInf_of_antitone records), and isRightContinuous_enlJoint holds. So aug is the null-set
  component of the usual augmentation, and as that it is correct: {A ∈ m₀ : A ~ B ∈ m} =
  σ(m ∪ 𝒩₀) for m ≤ m₀.
- Null sets: the μ-null sets inside the ambient m₀, not those of the completion. Lean's Ω has
  a single σ-algebra and every random variable is m₀-measurable, so non-m₀-measurable subsets of
  null sets cannot be seen by any process; this is the standard Lean-level form.
Verdict: faithful with representation choices.

verdict.detail:
Representation choices of aug, and why each is harmless:
1. aug augments a single σ-algebra by null sets; the right-continuity of the paper's "usual
   augmentation" is applied separately (enlJoint = augmentation of the right-continuous version,
   proved right-continuous), and σ(G_{t+} ∪ 𝒩) equals ⋂_{s>t} σ(G_s ∪ 𝒩), so the composite is the
   paper's filtration.
2. The null sets are the μ-null sets of the ambient σ-algebra m₀ rather than of its completion:
   all processes are measured against m₀, so the missing non-measurable null subsets change no
   adaptedness or measurability statement about them.

author_review.disagreements:
The author's review, as shown by rv.py author, consists of the review marker only (no reading text, no item-by-item comparison), so there is no stated position of the author to disagree with on substance.
Not recorded there: aug is only the null-set augmentation of one σ-algebra (no right limit) and
uses the null sets of the ambient σ-algebra, not of its completion; the paper's "usual
augmentation" is the composite enlJoint = aug of the right-continuous version, which is where
right-continuity comes from.
